source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet - section 4 debate vs self-consistency
finding: At the same number of model responses, plain majority voting over independent samples beats multi-agent debate. Debate is close to self-consistency only at 3 responses. Gap 1 answered for GPT-3.5 on GSM8K.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5-Turbo. Standard prompt (1 response) 76.7. Self-consistency 3 responses 82.5; 6 responses 85.3; 9 responses 88.2. Debate round 1 (6 responses) 83.2; round 2 (9 responses) 83.0. So at 9 responses debate is 5.2 points below voting, and its second round adds nothing.
quote: multi-agent debate significantly underperforms simple self-consistency using majority voting
limits: One older model (GPT-3.5), one math benchmark in this table. Responses are the cost unit, not tokens. Debate responses are longer (they carry peer text), so the token gap is probably larger.
agent_relevance: Spend a fixed budget on independent attempts then take the median or vote. Do not show attempts to each other unless a check says the exchange helps. Supports G4/G9.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet - sections 3.2-3.3 (intrinsic vs oracle self-correction)
finding: When a model re-reads its own earlier answer and may change it, accuracy falls. It only rises when the stopping rule uses the true label (an oracle). Gap 2 (own earlier attempts as the peer) and gap 6 (external check) both touched.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: standard 75.9; self-correct with oracle label 84.3; intrinsic round 1 (3 calls) 75.1; round 2 (5 calls) 74.7. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: standard 75.8; oracle 89.7; intrinsic round 1 38.1; round 2 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K: standard 95.5; oracle 97.5; intrinsic round 1 91.5; round 2 89.0. GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; of the changes, more go correct->incorrect than the reverse.
limits: The oracle row is not a deployable check; it only shows the upper bound. Models are 2023-era; newer reasoning models were not tested here.
agent_relevance: A verifier that is truly external (code run, test, exact check) is the only variant of revision that is supported. A revision judged by the same model is not. Supports G4 gating and the not-to-add list.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models? - Table 1 and martingale test
finding: Across seven benchmarks, majority voting over 5 independent initial answers (debate round 0) matches or beats all debate variants. Authors prove debate is a martingale on belief in the correct answer and show mean agent accuracy stays flat across rounds. Gap 1 answered directly for open 7-8B models with the same agents.
numbers: Average over 7 tasks, 5 agents, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9. Qwen2.5-7B: single agent 0.7205; decentralised debate T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050; sparse T=2 0.7330; centralised T=2 0.6551; majority vote 0.7691. Llama3.1-8B: single 0.6203; decentralised T=2 0.6929; T=5 0.6761; sparse T=2 0.6990; centralised T=2 0.6094; majority vote 0.7242. On Arithmetics (Qwen) vote 0.99 vs debate T=2 0.76.
quote: Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD
limits: Small open models, 512 token cap, about 300 questions per task. Debate costs more tokens than voting, so the equal-token gap is larger than shown. A closed-model GPT-4 check (appendix G) shows the same trend; I did not re-read it in detail.
agent_relevance: Default is isolated attempts plus an aggregate. Exchange has to earn its place against that baseline at equal budget.

source: Choi et al. (2025) Debate or Vote - Table 2 (belief-update interventions)
finding: Debate improves only when the update rule is biased toward correction. An oracle that locks any agent once it says the correct answer lifts the average by about 9 points. Prompting agents to follow the majority (Conformist) or to follow peers (Follower) lifts it by about 3 points. Gap 6 upper bound; gap 5 partial.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, 7 tasks, decentralised debate T=2: vanilla 0.7332 (Table 2 version), Conformist 0.7625, Follower 0.7629, oracle 0.8236. At T=5: vanilla 0.7084, Conformist 0.7524, Follower 0.7577, oracle 0.8289. Majority vote with no debate for the same model was 0.7691 in Table 1, so Conformist and Follower still land below plain voting at T=2.
limits: The oracle uses ground truth, so it is a ceiling, not a method. The practical variants use the majority as the signal, which is exactly the herd. They still do not beat no-debate voting.
agent_relevance: A gate that locks answers only when an external check passes is the real-world version of the oracle. The gain from a perfect gate is large (about 9 points); a majority-based gate gives about 3 and stays under pure voting.

source: Zhang, Cui, Chen, Wang, Zhang, Wang, Wu, Hu (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate - We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Five debate methods on 9 benchmarks and 4 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.1-70B, Claude-3.5-haiku) mostly do not beat Chain-of-Thought, and self-consistency with a similar call budget wins most cases where it applies. Gap 1 answered at scale.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, 6 LLM calls per method, 3 runs, temperature 1. MMLU: CoT 80.73, SC 82.13, SoM debate 74.73, ChatEval 79.13, AgentVerse 80.40. MMLU-Pro: CoT 62.80, SC 66.27, SoM 62.80. GSM8K: CoT 93.60, SC 95.67, SoM 94.93. MATH: CoT 72.87, SC 73.96, SoM 75.40, EoT 75.93. Across 36 model-by-dataset cells, SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cells (ANOVA at 0.05); Multi-Persona never. Debate methods did beat the plain single agent (SA) in general. SoM and EoT erase few errors and introduce many new ones (figure 4).
limits: Call count, not tokens, is matched; the token curves in section 3.3 show SC scales better with tokens. SC was not run on code tasks (no single answer to vote on).
agent_relevance: At equal calls, voting over independent samples is the strong baseline; most exchange protocols lose to it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate - section 4 Heter-MAD and Table 4
finding: Randomly assigning each agent either GPT-4o-mini or Llama3.1-70B (probability 0.5) lifts debate by 3-8% relative to running the same debate with one model. But the comparison baseline is the average of the two models, not the better one. Gap 8: unresolved against the best single model, and my own arithmetic says mixing does not beat it here.
numbers: Mean over 9 datasets. SoM-GPT 74.3, SoM-Llama 69.9, SoM-Heter 76.7 (+6.4% vs SoM average). CoT-Average of the two models 72.5. EoT-Heter 75.7 vs EoT average +8.2%. ChatEval-Heter +4.0%, AgentVerse-Heter +2.7%. My own calculation from their Table 3: GPT-4o-mini CoT alone averages 77.0 over the same 9 datasets, above SoM-Heter 76.7. So the mixed debate does not beat the stronger model run alone with CoT.
limits: The 77.0 figure is my arithmetic on the authors' Table 3 means; it is not reported by them. Only two model families.
agent_relevance: Mixing families helps debate compared with weak-model debate, but there is no evidence here that it beats the best single model at equal cost. Consistent with Barrera-Lemarchand d=0.88 (best self wins).

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate - Table 1
finding: Same models, with and without one round of seeing each other's answers. For weaker models, majority accuracy after debate is lower than the majority of the independent first answers. For GPT-4o-mini it is flat. Gap 1 with exact paired numbers.
numbers: 100 random questions per task, 5 seeds, 3 agents, 2 rounds, GPT-4o-mini / Llama-3.1-8B / Mistral-7B. Majority without debate -> after debate (CSQA / MMLU / GSM8K). 3x GPT: 75.6->74.8 / 81.4->82.2 / 94.0->94.4. 3x Llama: 63.0->58.6 / 61.6->57.8 / 87.6->84.2. 3x Mistral: 44.4->39.4 / 33.6->24.4 / 43.6->46.4. Mixed 2 Mistral + 1 Llama: 58.2->50.2 / 51.8->43.6 / 82.6->75.8. Single agents: GPT 74.8/82.6/93.2; Llama 57.0/55.6/76.4; Mistral 41.6/34.0/34.2.
limits: Which row is which model is read from the single-agent rows (my reading; the model symbols were lost in text extraction). Small N (100 per task). The debate prompt is the Du et al. one that shows peer answers and reasoning.
agent_relevance: For frontier-grade models the exchange is neutral; for weaker ones it hurts. No evidence of gain from exchange alone.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap - sections 6.1-6.2 (flips, social pressure, correctness payoff prompt)
finding: Models flip correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse. The flip rate is highest when the model is alone in its answer and falls as more peers agree. A prompt that tells the model it is paid for correctness did not reduce correct-to-incorrect flips. Gap 3 (prompt-level incentive) and gap 2 (conformity cost).
numbers: Figure 2: of agents that change answers, more go correct->incorrect than incorrect->correct across all groups. Figure 3: resistance falls in round 2. Figure 4: P(correct->incorrect) is largest with 0 agreeing peers and falls with 1 and 2 agreeing peers (read from plot, values not printed in text). Figure 5: the correctness-payoff prompt (a monetary-incentive framing borrowed from partisan-bias work) did not reduce correct->incorrect flips.
quote: does not appear to decrease the number of undesirable correct->incorrect flips
limits: The incentive is a prompt sentence about payment, not a real scoring rule with consequences, and not collective-outcome pay like Bazazi. Small models for most runs. Exact flip percentages are only in figures.
agent_relevance: A promise of reward in the prompt does not buy independence. If incentive structure is to matter it has to act through the selection rule (what is kept), not through words.

source: Wu, Li, Li (2025) Can LLM Agents Really Debate? A Controlled Study of Multi-Agent Debate in Logical Reasoning
finding: Controlled Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles with ground truth. Showing self-reported confidence to peers had no significant effect on agreement stability (coefficient 0.025, standard error 0.015). Strong models in an incorrect majority corrected themselves only about a third of the time; weak models almost never. Gap 5 (format) partial.
numbers: Regression on agreement stability, 745 observations, R2 0.290: confidence visible 0.025 (SE 0.015, n.s.), debate order 0.002 (n.s.), strong agent in minority -0.102 (p<0.001), initial chaos -0.117 (p<0.001). Agent in a correct majority stays correct above 97% for all models; agent in an incorrect majority corrects: gemini-2.5-flash 34.4%, gpt-5-mini 30.0%, gemini-2.5-flash-lite 3.6%. Debate raised instance accuracy (size 4: 17.3% to 69.3%; size 8: 3.3% to 36.0%) but there is no independent-voting arm in that table.
limits: Logic puzzle with a unique answer; the debate gain there is not compared with majority voting over first answers, so it cannot answer gap 1.
agent_relevance: Peer pressure is strong in a wrong majority, and visible confidence does not fix it. Correction ability tracks the model's own strength.

source: Kaesberg, Becker, Wahle, Ruas, Gipp (2025) Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Seven decision rules compared with all else held fixed. Voting beats consensus by up to 13.2% on reasoning tasks; consensus beats voting by 2.8% on knowledge tasks. More agents help; more discussion rounds before the vote hurt. Format test: sharing only candidate answers (Collective Improvement) helped, while sharing reasoning hurt. Gap 5 answered for open models.
numbers: StrategyQA, mean accuracy over decision rules: baseline discussion 58.3%; All-Agents-Drafting (every agent writes an independent draft first) 62.8% (+3.3 points); Collective Improvement (limited communication, exchange of possible solutions only) 65.7% (+7.4); critical response generator 59.4% (+1.1); reasoning response generator 51.9% (-6.4). Mean cosine similarity of final answers: baseline 0.888, AAD 0.870, CI 0.845, critical 0.843, reasoning 0.916. More diversity goes with higher accuracy, except for the critical prompt.
limits: Open 7-8B class models; three runs; one dataset in this table. Authors cite problem drift as a reason more rounds hurt.
agent_relevance: Candidate-only exchange with independent drafting first beats reasoning exchange. Keep attempts' reasoning private; share, at most, answers.

source: Yao, Shang, Du, He, Lian, Zhang, Su, Swamy, Qi (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Inter-agent sycophancy causes 'disagreement collapse', where a debate ends in agreement before reaching the right answer. Agents that drop a correct answer do so by echoing, not by new reasoning (r=0.902 between sycophancy score and abandoning-correct rate). Persona prompts moved accuracy by only a point or two. Gaps 2 and 9.
numbers: CommonsenseQA, Llama3.3-70B homogeneous 2-agent decentralised: disagreement collapse rate up to 86.36% with no gain over single agent. Qwen3-32B systems collapse less and beat single agents. Adding a judge: Qwen-Qwen 83.62% -> 86.65%, Qwen-Llama 81.00% -> 86.49%, collapse 81.71% -> 41.27% and 80.41% -> 35.51%. 3 agents beat 2 agents. Persona sweep Qwen-Qwen 45 configs: accuracy 81.98% to 83.87%, worst when both are 'peacemaker'. Mixed Qwen3-32B/Llama3-70B 81 configs: 78.95% to 82.06%, best when both 'troublemaker'. Judge collapse correlates with sycophancy r=0.639.
limits: Debaters see other debaters, not their own old attempts. Moderate sycophancy is not harmful in the best settings (a mix of peacemaker and troublemaker).
agent_relevance: Persona prompts are a weak lever (about 2 points). A separate judge helps more than persona tuning. Judge-driven collapse exists too, so the judge must not just copy the debaters.

source: Li, Lin, Xia, Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial?
finding: Self-MoA (many samples from only the top model, one aggregation call) beats a mix of different models in most settings. Output quality matters more than cross-model diversity. Gap 8 answered for aggregation (not debate) and gap 9 partly (temperature varied).
numbers: Self-MoA beats mixed MoA by 6.6 points on AlpacaEval 2.0 and 3.8 points on average over MMLU, CRUX, MATH. Regression of MoA score on diversity (Vendi score) and quality over 70+ proposer mixtures with temperature 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2: MMLU diversity coefficient 2.558 (SE 0.176), quality 1.841; CRUX 4.548 / 1.421; MATH 4.719 / 2.839; R2 0.771, 0.685, 0.760 (all p<0.001). At fixed quality more diversity helps; at fixed diversity more quality helps; mixing models usually lowers mean quality. Default sampling temperature 0.7.
limits: The aggregator reads all samples, so this is synthesis not voting. The diversity-quality regression is correlational over chosen mixtures. Mixing helps only in some task-specific cases (gains of 0.17% and 0.35% over Self-MoA).
agent_relevance: Take the best model and sample it many times. Within-model sampling diversity is enough. Do not add weaker families to get diversity.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? - section 3 agreement modulation
finding: Telling a debating agent how often to agree ('agree with the other agents X% of the time') changes accuracy a lot, and the best level depends on the task. High agreement helped MedQA and PubMedQA; the counter-intuitive CIAR set preferred disagreement. Gap 5 and gap 9 (a prompt-level control of herding).
numbers: USMLE subset (376 questions): tuning agreement intensity gave +15% for Multi-Persona and +5% for Society of Minds; ChatEval hardly changed. With 90% agreement, Multi-Persona went from worst protocol to best on MedQA, beating Medprompt and self-consistency. Debate protocols overall did not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling.
limits: Tuned on the test subset, so the +15% is optimistic. Exact figures are in plots. Needs a per-task setting. GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 era models.
agent_relevance: Agreement level is a hidden hyperparameter of any exchange step. A fixed exchange rule can help one task and hurt another, which argues against a standing rule that lets attempts see each other.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters - section 6 (sequential revisions vs parallel)
finding: For a model fine-tuned to revise, N sequential revisions (each sees the earlier attempts) narrowly beat N parallel independent samples at equal generation budget, with a verifier or with majority vote. A naive revision turns 38% of correct answers wrong, so selection is needed. The best split between sequential and parallel depends on difficulty: easy questions favour sequential, hard ones a mix. Gaps 1, 2 and 6 with a trained revise model.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S* revision model fine-tuned on up to 4 in-context wrong answers. About 38% of correct answers are converted back to incorrect by a naive revision step. Selecting by verifier or sequential majority fixes most of it. Figure 6 right: sequential beats parallel at equal budget under both selectors (narrowly; no numbers in text). Figure 7: the ideal sequential-to-parallel ratio varies by difficulty bin at budget 128.
limits: The model was trained to revise; an off-the-shelf model (d02) does not revise well. The verifier is a learned PRM, not an exact check. Numbers are read from plots.
agent_relevance: Own earlier attempts are different from peer answers: they come from the same distribution and are not a consensus. Revision can pay, but only with a trained reviser or a real selector, and the best mix shifts with difficulty. Supports a difficulty gate.

source: Xu, Zhu, Zhao, Pan, Li, Wang (2024) Pride and Prejudice: LLM Amplifies Self-Bias in Self-Refinement
finding: Six LLMs favour their own earlier output when judging it. Self-refinement makes fluent text but increases this self-bias. Larger models and external feedback with accurate assessment reduce it and give real gains. Gap 2 and gap 6.
numbers: Six models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini, Llama 2, Mixtral, DeepSeek) on translation, constrained generation and math reasoning. Self-bias found in all of them. Per-task bias scores not recorded here (abstract and introduction read).
limits: Judging tasks are mostly text quality; math effects are smaller. Tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: If an attempt reviews its own earlier attempt without outside facts, it tends to approve it. External feedback is the fix.

source: Park, Han, Guo, Ozdaglar, Zhang, Kim (2025) MAPoRL: Multi-Agent Post-Co-Training for Collaborative LLMs with Reinforcement Learning
finding: Off-the-shelf small LLMs do not improve over turns of discussion even with twice the output length. Training them with a shared verifier reward (correct final answer plus incentives for corrective and persuasive discussion) makes accuracy rise with turns. Tilting the reward changes revision behaviour. Gap 3: the only LLM test of a collective-outcome reward found, and it trains a policy; it is not a prompt.
numbers: Phi-3-mini (3.4B), also Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3-8B, QLoRA training, GSM8K and ANLI, 2 agents x 3 turns. Raising the reward weight for following a correct majority to 2 raised the measured gain in that transition by 9.5%; raising the weight for deviating from a wrong majority to 2 raised its measure by 2.57%; rewarding useful influence even when wrong gave a 17.2% improvement in the influence measure. Rewarding influence only when correct gave -1.32%.
limits: Small models, training required, accuracy axes in plots only. Reward is on the collective outcome, but the agents are trained, so it does not show whether telling a frozen model 'you are scored on the group' changes anything.
agent_relevance: Collective-outcome reward can shape revision in trained agents. For a frozen scaffold the analogue is a scoring rule on which attempts are kept, not a sentence in the prompt (see d08).

source: Renze & Guven (2024) The Effect of Sampling Temperature on Problem Solving in Large Language Models
finding: On multiple-choice problem solving, accuracy did not change significantly across temperature 0.0 to 1.0 for nine models and five prompt styles. It collapses above 1.0 (zero near 1.6). Gap 9: single-attempt accuracy is flat in temperature, so temperature is a free knob for the spread of attempts up to 1.0.
numbers: 1,000-question exam, GPT-3.5 with chain-of-thought, temperature 0.0 to 1.0: Kruskal-Wallis H(10)=10.439, p=0.403. 100-question exam over nine LLMs, five prompt techniques, temperature 0 to 1.6. Llama 2 7B near random. Performance drops quickly after 1.0.
limits: Single-attempt accuracy only; does not test aggregation or exchange. Multiple choice, not numeric estimation. Small exam sizes (acknowledged by the authors).
agent_relevance: Raising temperature up to about 1.0 widens the attempt spread at no accuracy cost. Whether the aggregate gains is the untested part of gap 9.

source: Wang, Wei, Schuurmans, Le, Chi, Narang, Chowdhery, Zhou (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models - robustness section and appendix A.1.1
finding: Voting over sampled reasoning paths works across temperature and top-k settings; accuracy rises with more paths for every setting tried. Gap 9 from the founding paper of the independent-sampling baseline.
numbers: LaMDA-137B on GSM8K, up to 40 sampled paths; settings T=0.3, 0.5, 0.7 with k=40; T=0.5 with k=20 and no top-k; all beat greedy decoding and rise with path count. Main experiments use T=0.5 for UL2-20B and LaMDA-137B. The paper states self-consistency is generally robust to sampling strategies and parameters.
limits: Old models, only a few temperatures, curves read from a figure caption and text.
agent_relevance: The independent-samples aggregate is not fragile to temperature; the exchange arms are the ones with hidden hyperparameters (d13).

source: Cui, Fu, Zhang, Wang, Zuo (2025) FREE-MAD: Consensus-Free Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Telling agents to be anti-conformist and scoring the whole debate trajectory (not just the last-round vote) improves on the standard Society-of-Minds debate in one round. Gap 5 and gap 3 (a decision rule that discounts herding).
numbers: 8 benchmarks, N=4 (Qwen1.5-7B-Chat plus Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) or N=3 for AIME (Qwen1.5-7B plus DeepSeek-V3), one debate round. Anti-conformity plus score decision vs SoM baseline: GSM-Level4 73.75 vs 60.00; GSM-Level6 70.00 vs 52.50; AIME2024 53.33 vs 33.33; AIME2025 43.33 vs 26.67; MATH500 65.00 vs 65.00; Logical Fallacies 70.00 vs 66.25; AICrypto 75.00 vs 63.75; StrategyQA 65.00 vs 65.00. Variant with conformity plus score: 65.00, 61.25, 43.33, 36.67, 66.25, 72.50, 75.00, 71.25.
limits: Compared only with debate baselines, not with independent sampling at equal tokens. Small test sets (AIME has 30 questions, so the 20-point differences are a handful of items). Numbers read from the bar-chart text layer; column order inferred.
agent_relevance: Cheap evidence that herd pressure can be dampened by prompt plus a rule that does not trust the last round. Still untested against plain voting.

source: Da & Huang (2020) Harnessing the Wisdom of Crowds, Management Science (Estimize.com field data and randomised experiments)
finding: A large real-world, non-student result in the Lorenz direction: forecasters who viewed more public estimates weighted their own information less, individual forecasts got better, the consensus got worse. Randomised experiments that hid public information from random users and stocks confirmed that independent forecasts give a more accurate consensus. The platform then switched to a blind design in November 2015. Gap 7: closest field support.
numbers: Earnings-forecast platform; sample sizes are not in the abstract record I read.
limits: Only the Crossref abstract record was read, not the full paper, so opened is false and no numbers are recorded. It tests earnings forecasts by self-selected analysts, not the Lorenz questions, so it is a conceptual, not a direct, replication.
agent_relevance: Real data in which individual gain and collective loss coexist, as in K02. Supports keeping first-round attempts blind.

source: Mercier & Claidiere (2022) Does discussion make crowds any wiser? Cognition 222:104912
finding: Large-group discussion (not just seeing numbers) did not hurt, and often helped, aggregation for problems with a correct answer. Boundary to Lorenz: free discussion of reasons, problems with logical or factual answers. Gap 7 boundary (not a null replication of the numeric-estimate design).
numbers: N=1,958 participants in groups of 22 to 212 (mean 59); three problem types (demonstrative, factual, ethical). Demonstrative: discussion improved individual answers and the aggregate. Factual: improved individual answers; aggregate improved or unchanged.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC), so opened is false. Reasons were exchanged, which Lorenz did not allow; problems were not skewed numeric estimates.
agent_relevance: Exchanging reasons on problems with checkable answers can help the aggregate. This is the human analogue of verifier-gated exchange rather than blind number-copying.
